title: Reverse Signaling: When the Ligand Is Also a Receptor

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Human pro-EGF is a 1,207-amino-acid membrane-spanning precursor whose 53-amino-acid EGF peptide sits just outside the membrane, where {{c1::proteases}} cut it free.
cards.why: Pro-EGF contains a signal peptide, a long outer region, one transmembrane segment, and a cytosolic tail before proteolytic cleavage releases mature EGF.
cards.quote: The 53 amino acids of EGF sit just outside the membrane, where proteases cut them free.
cards.section: Why a ligand starts out as a large membrane protein

cards.front: Why did finding that ligands such as pro-EGF, TNF, Fas ligand, and Delta are synthesized as membrane proteins suggest that some ligands might also act as receptors?
cards.back: Making a ligand as a transmembrane protein gives it a cytosolic tail inside its own cell, the structural feature expected of a signaling receptor.
cards.why: While pro-EGF's large precursor is still not fully explained, having an intracellular tail equips membrane ligands to potentially transmit signals inward.
cards.quote: giving each "ligand" a tail inside its own cell, the feature you expect of a receptor.
cards.section: Why a ligand starts out as a large membrane protein

cards.front: Mature EGF is 53 amino acids long, whereas human pro-EGF is 1,207 amino acids long. About how many times longer is pro-EGF than mature EGF, and what percentage of the precursor becomes the released EGF peptide?
cards.back: Setup: 1,207 / 53 ≈ 22.8 times longer; (53 / 1,207) × 100 ≈ 4.4%. Human pro-EGF is more than twenty times longer than the mature peptide released by proteases.
cards.quote: Yet when mouse EGF mRNA was cloned in 1983, it predicted a membrane-spanning protein more than twenty times longer.
cards.section: Why a ligand starts out as a large membrane protein

cards.front: When two touching cells interact via a receptor and a membrane-bound ligand, the message into the receptor's cell is the forward signal and the message into the ligand's cell is {{c1::reverse signaling}}.
cards.back: Together, forward and reverse signaling form bidirectional signaling.
cards.quote: The message into the receptor's cell is the forward signal; a second message into the ligand's cell is reverse signaling.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: What two requirements must a ligand meet to send a reverse signal into its own cell?
cards.back: It must stay attached to its cell's membrane and reach the cytosol via either its own tail or a membrane neighbour.
cards.quote: A reverse signal requires two things: the ligand must stay attached to its cell and reach the cytosol via its own tail or a membrane neighbour.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: In bidirectional contact-dependent signaling, what do the labels "ligand" and "receptor" actually reflect?
cards.back: They record only which role each protein was first observed to play, not which cell receives a signal.
cards.why: Like a handshake, neither partner can grip the other without being gripped, so both proteins can send and receive signals.
cards.quote: the names "ligand" and "receptor" record only which role each protein was first seen to play.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: Why does strong conservation of a membrane-bound ligand's cytosolic tail from fish to mammals suggest reverse signaling?
cards.back: A functionless tail drifts over evolution, so strong conservation across species points to cytosolic binding partners and an inward signaling function.
cards.quote: A functionless tail drifts over evolution, so strong conservation across species suggests cytosolic partners and an inward signal.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: Why is being a contact-dependent membrane-anchored ligand insufficient by itself to prove reverse signaling?
cards.back: Some membrane-bound contact ligands signal only one way: Notch also needs two touching cells, yet the signal runs one way, into the Notch-bearing cell.
cards.quote: Contact alone is not proof, however: Notch also needs two touching cells, yet in the Notch lesson the signal runs one way, into the Notch-bearing cell.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: A membrane-anchored ligand triggers bidirectional signaling when it contacts a receptor on a neighbouring cell. If a protease cleaves the ligand's outer domain free from the membrane, what happens to reverse signaling and why?
cards.back: Reverse signaling ends. Once cleaved free, the ligand is no longer attached to its own cell and cannot transmit receptor binding to its cytosolic tail or membrane partner.
cards.quote: Proteolytic cleavage ends reverse signaling, and inner-route mutations still require controls for surface expression, direct forward signaling, and receptor redundancy.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: Which major biological processes use reverse signaling?
cards.back: Cell migration and proliferation, axon guidance, angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels), the immune response, apoptosis, and development.
cards.quote: Reverse signaling acts in cell migration and proliferation, axon guidance, angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels), the immune response, apoptosis, and development.
cards.section: Forward, reverse, and bidirectional signaling

cards.front: Eph receptors form the largest receptor tyrosine kinase family, with {{c1::14}} members in humans.
cards.quote: Their Eph receptors are the largest receptor tyrosine kinase family (14 members in humans).
cards.section: Ephrins: borrowing a kinase or a partner

cards.front: How do A-type and B-type ephrins differ in how they attach to the plasma membrane?
cards.back: Five A-type ephrins attach to the outer leaflet via a GPI anchor (no cytosolic tail); three B-type ephrins span the membrane once with an 83- to 93-amino-acid tail.
cards.quote: the three B-type ephrins cross the membrane once and end in an 83- to 93-amino-acid cytosolic tail.
cards.section: Ephrins: borrowing a kinase or a partner

cards.front: Although EphA and EphB receptors match their preferred ephrin classes, some cross classes—for example, {{c1::EphA4}} also binds B-type ephrins.
cards.quote: EphA and EphB receptors match their preferred ligands, though some cross classes: EphA4 also binds B-type ephrins.
cards.section: Ephrins: borrowing a kinase or a partner

cards.front: A B-type ephrin tail has no enzyme activity. What two conserved signaling features does it contain?
cards.back: Conserved tyrosines shared across all three B-type ephrins and a C-terminal motif that fits PDZ domains.
cards.quote: The B-ephrin tail holds no enzyme, only conserved tyrosines shared across all three B-type ephrins and a C-terminal motif fitting PDZ domains
cards.section: B-type ephrins: two routes on one short tail

cards.front: Cells making a transmembrane B-type ephrin (which has no kinase domain) and no Eph receptor are treated with the purified outer domain of an EphB receptor (which lacks its kinase domain). The ephrin tail gains phosphotyrosine, and a Src-family kinase inhibitor blocks this band. What does this show?
cards.back: A Src-family kinase inside the ephrin's own cell phosphorylates the ephrin tail after receptor binding, because neither the ephrin nor the soluble EphB outer fragment contains a kinase domain.
cards.quote: proving a kinase inside the ephrin's own cell acted, since neither the receptor fragment nor the ephrin had a kinase domain.
cards.section: B-type ephrins: two routes on one short tail

cards.front: How do Src-family kinases and PTP-BL act as opposing switches on the B-type ephrin tail after EphB clustering?
cards.back: Src-family kinases gather at clustered B-ephrins as positive regulators of tail tyrosine phosphorylation, and after a delay the tyrosine phosphatase PTP-BL binds the PDZ-binding end to remove those phosphates.
cards.quote: Src-family kinases gather at EphB-clustered B-ephrins as positive regulators of tail phosphorylation
cards.section: B-type ephrins: two routes on one short tail

cards.front: The adaptor protein {{c1::Grb4}} binds phosphotyrosines on the B-type ephrin tail via its SH2 domain, linking ephrin-B to proteins that reshape the actin cytoskeleton.
cards.quote: the adaptor Grb4 binds those phosphotyrosines via its SH2 domain, linking ephrin-B to proteins that reshape the actin cytoskeleton.
cards.section: B-type ephrins: two routes on one short tail

cards.front: In mouse ephrin-B2, what happens to tail signaling and dephosphorylation if a mutation deletes only the C-terminal PDZ-binding end while leaving all five conserved tyrosines intact?
cards.back: PDZ-dependent signaling would be lost and PTP-BL, which binds the PDZ end, could no longer remove the phosphates; Src-family phosphorylation and SH2-adaptor (Grb4) binding would be expected to remain.
cards.why: Because PTP-BL binds the PDZ-binding end to remove tail phosphates, deleting that motif disables both the PDZ output branch and its phosphatase-mediated turn-off.
cards.quote: after a delay the tyrosine phosphatase PTP-BL binds the PDZ-binding end to remove the phosphates.
cards.section: B-type ephrins: two routes on one short tail

cards.front: In mouse ephrin-B2, deleting the C-terminal PDZ-binding end causes major lymphatic malformations, whereas mutating all five conserved tail tyrosines to phenylalanine causes only a mild lymphatic defect. What does this split show?
cards.back: Lymphatic remodeling depends mainly on the PDZ-binding branch rather than tyrosine phosphorylation, demonstrating that tissue context decides which B-ephrin tail route dominates.
cards.quote: Src-family phosphorylation is central to B-ephrin reverse signaling, yet tissue context decides which tail route dominates.
cards.section: B-type ephrins: two routes on one short tail

cards.front: Why can a GPI-anchored ligand such as an A-type ephrin not directly signal to cytosolic proteins on its own?
cards.back: Held in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane with no transmembrane segment and no cytosolic tail, it never touches the cytosol and must couple inward through membrane partners.
cards.quote: held in the outer leaflet, it never touches the cytosol, so it must couple inward through partners that vary by cell type.
cards.section: How a GPI-anchored ephrin signals without a tail

cards.front: How does clustering GPI-anchored ephrin-A5 with the outer domain of an EphA receptor alter cell adhesion?
cards.back: Clustered ephrin-A5 collects in cholesterol-rich patches above inner-leaflet Src-family kinases, drawing Fyn into those patches and altering cell adhesion in a Fyn-dependent way.
cards.quote: clustering ephrin-A5 with the outer part of an EphA receptor drew Fyn into these patches and altered cell adhesion in a Fyn-dependent way.
cards.section: How a GPI-anchored ephrin signals without a tail

cards.front: Clustered EphA outer-domain reagent is added to retinal axons lacking the transmembrane neurotrophin receptor p75. What happens to outer binding versus intracellular Fyn phosphorylation, and why?
cards.back: EphA still binds ephrin-A on the outer leaflet, but Fyn phosphorylation and reverse signaling fail. Ephrin-A itself is intact, yet retinal axons require p75 as the transmembrane bridge to the cytosol.
cards.quote: In retinal axons, ephrin-A pairs with p75, a membrane-spanning neurotrophin receptor required there for reverse signaling and Fyn phosphorylation.
cards.section: How a GPI-anchored ephrin signals without a tail

cards.front: What mechanistic question remains unsettled about reverse signaling by GPI-anchored proteins such as A-type ephrins?
cards.back: How clustering an outer-leaflet protein activates an inner-leaflet kinase across the lipid bilayer when no transmembrane partner is present.
cards.quote: How an outer-leaflet protein activates an inner-leaflet kinase without a transmembrane partner remains unsettled (for GFR-alpha-1 and Ret, see Going deeper).
cards.section: How a GPI-anchored ephrin signals without a tail

cards.front: Why is a full gene knockout of either a membrane-bound ligand or its receptor ambiguous in a bidirectional signaling system?
cards.back: A full knockout removes forward signaling, reverse signaling, and physical cell-to-cell grip simultaneously, so a defect cannot distinguish which of those three caused it.
cards.quote: why a full knockout confounds forward signaling, reverse signaling, and cell-to-cell grip
cards.section: Separating forward from reverse signaling

cards.front: To separate bidirectional signals between two touching cells, disable one {{c1::inner route}} while keeping binding intact.
cards.quote: Applying the second half of the guiding rule—disable one inner route while keeping binding—yields a clean diagnostic table for a single pair:
cards.section: Separating forward from reverse signaling

cards.front: A tail-less mutant of a transmembrane ligand is made to test reverse signaling, but the truncated protein is trapped inside the cell instead of reaching the plasma membrane. What happens to forward signaling, reverse signaling, and grip, and what can you conclude?
cards.back: Forward signaling, reverse signaling, and cell-to-cell grip are all lost, making the mutant equivalent to a full knockout. Reverse signaling cannot be isolated unless normal cell-surface expression is confirmed.
cards.quote: before interpreting a truncated protein, confirm it reaches the cell surface in normal amounts
cards.section: Separating forward from reverse signaling

cards.front: Even when a tail-edited membrane ligand reaches the cell surface in normal amounts, why must you still measure forward signaling directly?
cards.back: Altering a ligand's cytosolic tail can change the forward signal sent into the receptor's cell—in one ephrin-B2 study even making forward signaling stronger.
cards.quote: changing the ephrin-B2 tail can alter the forward signal in the receptor's cell—in one case making it stronger—so measure forward signaling directly.
cards.section: Separating forward from reverse signaling

cards.front: In a tissue co-expressing EphB2 and EphB3, a mouse expresses kinase-less EphB2 at normal surface levels. Predict what can happen to forward signaling, and explain why a normal phenotype does not rule out a requirement for forward signaling.
cards.back: Forward signaling can remain active, so the tissue may appear normal. Kinase-less EphB2 can co-cluster with intact EphB3—or EphB3 can substitute directly—so ruling out forward signaling may require disabling multiple EphB genes.
cards.quote: Kinase-less EphB2 can co-cluster with intact EphB3—or EphB3 can substitute directly—keeping forward signaling active.
cards.section: Separating forward from reverse signaling

cards.front: Why can you not isolate reverse signaling in GPI-anchored A-type ephrins by truncating the ligand's tail, and what perturbation in retinal axons disables reverse signaling while preserving outer EphA binding?
cards.back: Tail truncation cannot be used because, by the GPI-anchor rule, A-type ephrins sit in the outer leaflet with no cytosolic tail; applying the rule to disable one inner route while keeping binding means removing the transmembrane bridge (p75 in retinal axons), which abolishes Fyn phosphorylation and reverse signaling while leaving EphA–ephrin-A binding intact.
cards.quote: Applying the second half of the guiding rule—disable one inner route while keeping binding—yields a clean diagnostic table for a single pair:
cards.section: Separating forward from reverse signaling

cards.front: How do you genetically remove reverse signaling from a transmembrane ligand while keeping forward signaling intact, and what two controls must accompany the experiment?
cards.back: Keep the ligand's outer domain and transmembrane segment while replacing its cytosolic tail (such as with beta-galactosidase). Confirm normal surface levels to prevent intracellular-trapping artefacts, and measure forward signaling directly.
cards.quote: Run two controls: confirm normal surface levels (preventing intracellular-trapping artefacts), and measure forward signaling directly
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How can you disable only one reverse-signaling branch of the ephrin-B2 tail at a time rather than replacing the entire tail?
cards.back: Mutate the five conserved tyrosines to phenylalanine to block tyrosine phosphorylation while sparing the PDZ end, or delete the C-terminal PDZ residue to remove only the PDZ branch.
cards.quote: Finer alleles mutate the five conserved tyrosines to phenylalanine or delete the C-terminal PDZ residue, removing one route at a time.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In dissecting reverse signaling, how does stimulating ligand-bearing cells with clustered soluble receptor-Fc complement a tail-less ligand knock-in mouse?
cards.back: With no receptor cell present, a ligand-dependent response to receptor-Fc (absent with Fc alone) tests sufficiency, whereas the tail-less knock-in mouse tests necessity.
cards.quote: a ligand-dependent response (absent with Fc alone) tests sufficiency, while the knock-in mouse tests necessity.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mice lacking a receptor tyrosine kinase have an axon-guidance defect in a brain tract whose axons express its membrane-bound ligand and no receptor, while the cells they grow across express the receptor. Mice expressing a kinase-less receptor at normal surface levels have a normal tract. What does this show, and what caveat remains?
cards.back: By the inner-route dissection rule, a normal tract without the receptor's kinase rules out forward signaling via that kinase alone and indicates its outer domain acts as a ligand triggering reverse signaling into the axons—subject to the caveat of receptor heteroclustering and redundancy among related receptors.
cards.quote: Disabling the receptor's kinase while keeping its outer domain (as Henkemeyer's 1996 EphB2 mouse did in the anterior commissure) tests forward signaling
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: For a single membrane ligand–receptor pair, a full ligand knockout has a defect that neither a surface-expressed tail-less ligand mouse nor a surface-expressed kinase-less receptor mouse shows. What two interpretations remain, and how does a double-altered mouse distinguish them?
cards.back: By the bidirectional dissection rules, either forward and reverse signaling are redundant (either direction suffices) or plain physical grip suffices. A double-altered mouse (tail-less ligand plus kinase-less receptor, both at the surface) separates them: normal means adhesion suffices; defective means redundant signaling was required.
cards.quote: A double-altered mouse (tail-less ephrin plus kinase-less receptor) separates them: normal means adhesion suffices; defective means redundant signaling was required.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Membrane-bound TNF is a three-chain protein with 35-amino-acid cytosolic tails whose outer trimer can be cut free by the protease TACE. Predict how inhibiting TACE on developing sympathetic axons would affect reverse TNF signaling versus soluble forward TNF signaling, and state the rule.
cards.back: Reverse signaling into the axons would be expected to be preserved, while soluble forward signaling by released TNF would be reduced. Uncut membrane TNF can receive a reverse signal, whereas TACE cleavage breaks that inward link while leaving the released trimer free to signal forward.
cards.quote: uncut membrane TNF can receive a reverse signal, whereas TACE cleavage breaks that inward link while leaving released TNF free to signal forward.
cards.section: TNF and semaphorins: other ligands that listen

cards.front: What phosphorylation change occurs on membrane TNF's tail upon soluble TNF receptor binding, and why is the CK1 motif described only as "likely" essential?
cards.back: A tail serine in a casein kinase 1 (CK1) motif loses phosphate when soluble TNF receptor binds; it is called "likely" essential because evidence comes mainly from one macrophage study.
cards.why: The CK1 site is a short sequence motif shared across several TNF-family tails rather than a catalytic domain, and the phosphorylation-loss evidence comes mainly from one study of membrane TNF in mouse macrophages.
cards.quote: because it is a short motif rather than a catalytic domain and the evidence comes mainly from one study of membrane TNF in mouse macrophage cells.
cards.section: TNF and semaphorins: other ligands that listen

cards.front: Mice lacking either TNF or TNFR1 both show sparser sympathetic innervation of target tissues. Why are those knockouts ambiguous alone, and what culture result settled the signaling direction?
cards.back: By the full-knockout ambiguity rule, losing either partner predicts the same phenotype under forward or reverse signaling. Pairing those knockouts with the soluble-receptor sufficiency rule—soluble TNFR1 boosted sympathetic axon growth and branching in culture only when membrane TNF was present—settled that target TNFR1 signals inward through axonal membrane TNF.
cards.quote: Pairing that result with soluble TNFR1 in culture (which boosted axon growth and branching only when membrane TNF was present) settled the direction:
cards.section: TNF and semaphorins: other ligands that listen

cards.front: Sympathetic neurons are cultured with or without soluble TNFR1-Fc (no receptor cells present). Mean axon lengths without vs. with TNFR1-Fc are: wild-type, 250 µm vs. 350 µm; TNFR1-knockout, 250 µm vs. 350 µm; TNF-knockout, 250 µm vs. 250 µm. What is the percentage increase in wild-type axon length, and which protein must the neuron carry for the reagent to work?
cards.back: Setup: ((350 − 250) / 250) × 100 = 40% increase. The neuron must carry membrane TNF (TNF-knockout fails to respond) and does not need TNFR1 (TNFR1-knockout still increases by 40%), showing reverse signaling through axonal TNF.
cards.quote: Developing sympathetic axons carry membrane TNF while target tissues make TNF receptor 1 (TNFR1).
cards.section: TNF and semaphorins: other ligands that listen

cards.front: In fruit fly motor axons, the cytoplasmic tail of transmembrane Sema-1a binds a GEF and a GAP that regulate the small GTPase {{c1::Rho}}.
cards.quote: In motor axons, Sema-1a's tail binds two regulators of the small GTPase Rho, a GEF and a GAP (see the lesson on GTPase switches).
cards.section: TNF and semaphorins: other ligands that listen

cards.front: In the fruit fly eye, losing either Sema-1a or its receptor plexin A disrupts axon bundling. What single alteration to Sema-1a (with its control) tests whether Sema-1a acts as a receptor receiving a reverse signal?
cards.back: Delete or replace Sema-1a's cytoplasmic tail while confirming its outer domain reaches the axon surface at normal levels; persistent bundling defects show that Sema-1a's inward tail route is required.
cards.quote: Delete or replace Sema-1a's cytoplasmic tail while confirming its outer domain reaches the axon surface at normal levels.
cards.section: TNF and semaphorins: other ligands that listen

cards.front: Human TNF is made as a 233-amino-acid membrane protein with a 35-amino-acid cytosolic tail, and a protease releases the outer 157 amino acids. How many amino acids remain cell-associated after cleavage, and how many of those lie outside the cytosolic tail?
cards.back: Setup: 233 − 157 = 76 amino acids remain with the cell after cleavage; 76 − 35 = 41 of those lie outside the cytosolic tail.
cards.quote: TNF is made as a 233-amino-acid membrane protein from which a protease releases the outer 157.
cards.section: How big is the EGF precursor, and which other ligands are made this way?

cards.front: Once its signal peptide is removed, the human EGF precursor is 1,185 amino acids long—almost the same length as the finished human {{c1::EGF receptor}} (1,186 amino acids).
cards.quote: The finished human EGF receptor has 1,186 amino acids, and the EGF precursor has 1,185 once its signal peptide is removed.
cards.section: How big is the EGF precursor, and which other ligands are made this way?

cards.front: GPI-anchored GFR-alpha-1 normally passes GDNF signals to the transmembrane kinase Ret, yet can also activate Src-family kinases in cells lacking Ret. Based on membrane topology rules for GPI-anchored ligands, what unresolved problem does this share with ephrin-A, and how does retinal-axon ephrin-A signaling differ?
cards.back: GPI-anchored proteins sit only in the outer leaflet with no transmembrane segment or cytosolic tail, so both GFR-alpha-1 without Ret and ephrin-A without a transmembrane partner raise the same unresolved question of how an outer-leaflet protein activates an inner-leaflet Src-family kinase. In retinal axons, ephrin-A pairs with p75, a membrane-spanning neurotrophin receptor required there for reverse signaling.
cards.quote: yet can also activate Src-family kinases without Ret—raising the same unresolved bilayer-crossing question as ephrin-A.
cards.section: Another GPI-anchored protein that borrows a partner

cards.front: Semaphorins span eight classes (secreted, membrane-spanning, and one GPI-anchored) that signal primarily with plexins and all share a conserved ~500-amino-acid outer {{c1::sema domain}}.
cards.quote: All share a ~500-amino-acid outer sema domain, highly conserved across classes, and signal primarily with plexins.
cards.section: The semaphorin family and its sema domain
